patch.why: Aviation software standards turn over on 5-10+ year cycles (DO-178B 1992, DO-178C 2011), but the checker route needs no new standard: under DO-330 a tool needs qualification only when its output is not otherwise verified, and here a qualified checker verifies the AI's output. 'Achieved' means plan acceptance, which is the study's base-case premise for first certification credit (S2 2030, S3 2029). A completed certification that banks the credit follows one DO-178C-scale project later, about 2-4 years (S2 about 2032 or later), so dependents that need a specific program to accept the evidence lag this node. Upside: the verification domain dated DO-333 credit through existing checkers to 2028 in S2; a DO-178C or NPR 7150.2 plan accepted in 2028-29 would pull this node forward a year. Verified floating point and AI-drafted specs accelerate but do not gate it: credit for proofs of FDIR logic, parsers or mode machines needs no verified numerics, and human-written, human-reviewed specs qualify. Capped at Medium by 2031 because it needs regulator acceptance; High by 2035 because the route runs through a mechanism already in use (DO-333 credit through already-qualified checkers).

Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous anchor on launch, satellite production, chip supply and capital, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. At 16,000-18,000 t per GW today, or about 10,000 t at 100 kW/t, 10 GW is 100,000-180,000 t: about 700-1,800 Starship flights at 100-150 t to low orbit, and more to dawn-dusk orbit, where each flight from Florida carries roughly 20-30% less (assumption). Only the Florida pads reach these orbits; Starbase cannot fly south. At a third to a half of 300 flights a year and 100-150 t per flight, compute gets 0.6-2.3 GW a year. Chain (S3): 1 GW in 2031 -> 300+ heavy flights a year from 2032 (capability-35-heavy-cadence-300) -> cadence keeps growing by about 100 flights a year -> compute takes about half -> Starship V4 lifts about 150 t to dawn-dusk orbit and new satellites reach 100 kW/t -> 3-4 GW a year by 2034-35 -> 10 GW in 2035. Every link is an upside case. S2 runs a year behind on cadence and reaches 10 GW only after 2035. A rough simulation on the trunk's launch clock (calculation, ranges as above) puts a central case near 5-6 GW at end-2035 in S3 and 4-5 GW in S2. Chips and packaging co-bind: about 2.9 million GPU packages at 250 kW per 72-GPU satellite. Capital is large but reachable: Mach33's base case puts orbital capex at $46B per GW, falling toward $24B over a decade, so 10 GW is roughly $240-460B (a single commercial forecaster's model). Mach33's own reference reaches 10 GW in 2032, but on a launch clock about three times faster than the model's trunk. AI math is second-order: hotter chips, lighter radiators and right-sized radiation mitigation cut launched mass by a few percent to about 10%. S4 gets no credit. Robot-built pads and plants arrive only about 2035 in Embodied (Low), too late to add launch capacity before end-2035.2-2 GW by end-2035 (calculation); that leaves S4 at Low, and airspace, approvals, chips and capital do not compress. Satellite and array lines already run ahead of flights. Bands (judgment): S3 and S4 Low by 2035; S2 and S1 Speculative, after 2035.

Checking sets the price. Only about a third of a program's critical path is thinking work, so base-case schedule cuts top out near 38%. Realized gains are likelier 20-30%.

patch.thesis: If AI settles famous fluid problems, almost no engine, heat shield or orbit changes. Engineers get proof tools and on-demand error bars from about 2028 (base case). patch.reader_hook: An AI agent formalized a plasma physics result (Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau) in 10 days for about $200, with no human-written code (one mathematician, 229 prompts). Two of its three failure modes came from stating the problem. Only 16 of the release's 372 families concern partial differential equations and 12 concern dynamics, reflecting which problems the lab chose to pose.

Certified flow and materials models give engines reuse life by analysis from about 2029 (base case). Hot fire and flights set the pace. patch.reader_hook: A reusable rocket engine spends about 3-6 minutes at full temperature per flight, up to about 5 hours over 50 flights, so rigs can life-test its hot parts in weeks. Reliability takes longer: 0.99 at 90% confidence needs about 230 independent zero-failure starts. One Starship flight logs about 65-70 starts, but they share a vehicle and a build lot.

But it sampled heating error only up to existing margins, while at that 8 km/s entry the radiation model under-predicted shock-tube data by up to 2x.

Qualifying chips to run about 30 C hotter saves about 1,900 t per GW (33FG model).
